mainTopic: Which oxen make a pit owner liable, and how the תורה's 'ox and donkey' laws extend to all animals
overview: The amud opens by asking whether the משנה implies that a smart, normal ox falling into a pit leaves the owner exempt. רבי ירמיה says no: the משנה only lists the weak oxen because they are the surprising case. רב אחא challenges this with ברייתות about a 'בר דעת' falling in, and in the end רבא sets רבי ירמיה's reading aside. He rules that only a deaf, foolish, young, blind or night-walking ox makes the owner liable, because a normal ox should watch where it goes. A new משנה then teaches that many laws written about an 'ox' or 'donkey' apply to every animal, wild animal and bird. The גמרא finds a source for each law, and many of them are linked to שבת through a גזירה שוה. It proves from the extra words 'וכל בהמתך' in the second עשרת הדברות that שבת covers all creatures, working through כלל ופרט and ריבוי along the way. It also explains why people, who appear in the same שבת verse, may still plow alongside an animal. The amud ends as רבי חנינא בן עגיל begins asking why the word 'good' appears only in the second version of the עשרת הדברות, and his question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Would a smart ox be exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the משנה that a smart ox falling into a pit might leave the owner exempt, and questions that inference.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that if a smart, normal ox fell in, the pit owner would be exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the משנה's list of a deaf, foolish or young ox and asks a pointed question: does that mean a normal, smart ox would make the pit owner exempt?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only mentions weak or limited oxen as causing liability. Reading closely, that seems to imply a healthy ox would not. That sounds backwards, since a pit is just as dangerous to any ox.

keyTerms.meaning: But this implies; introduces an inference from the text

phrases.english: But then, an ox that is smart, would he be exempt?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is reading this into the משנה, which listed only a deaf, foolish or young ox as making the pit owner liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion by challenging an implication of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's wording listing only a deaf, foolish or young ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only limited oxen are listed as causing liability, the משנה seems to suggest a smart ox would leave the owner exempt, which seems wrong.

steps.title: Rabbi Yirmeya: 'It goes without saying'
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה explains that a smart ox obviously makes the owner liable. The משנה teaches the newer point that even a limited ox does too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: the משנה is speaking in a 'no need to say' style. There is no need to say that a smart ox makes the owner liable. But with a deaf, foolish or young ox, you might think its own deafness or youth made it fall, so the owner should be exempt. The משנה teaches us that he is still liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers that the משנה never meant to exempt a smart ox. It deliberately lists the harder cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A smart ox falling in is the obvious case for liability. With a limited ox, one could argue that its own weakness caused the fall, not the pit, so the owner should be exempt. The משנה lists those cases to teach that even then the pit owner pays.

keyTerms.meaning: It goes without saying; not only this, but even that

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי ירמיה, the משנה lists the weak oxen as the surprising case, and a smart ox is obviously included. Be careful: רבא later rejects this (step 8) and rules that a normal, alert ox leaves the pit owner exempt.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
It is speaking in a 'there is no need to say' style;

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִבַּעְיָא שׁוֹר שֶׁהוּא פִּקֵּחַ – דְּחַיָּיב;
phrases.english: there is no need to say that for a smart ox he is liable;
but an ox that is deaf, foolish or young,
I might say its deafness caused it to fall,
its young age caused it, so he should be exempt;
so it teaches us that he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: לָא מִיבַּעְיָא קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the inference raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the משנה in a 'not only this, but even that' style
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A limited ox's own weakness caused the fall, so the pit owner should be exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The pit owner is liable even for a limited ox, and certainly for a smart one.

steps.title: רב אחא quotes a ברייתא exempting a 'בר דעת'
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא challenges רבינא with a ברייתא that exempts the pit owner when a 'בר דעת' falls in, which seems to mean a smart ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא said to רבינא: But a ברייתא teaches that if a 'בר דעת' (mentally competent one) fell into the pit, the owner is exempt. Doesn't that mean a mentally competent ox?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא brings a ברייתא that seems to say exactly what רבי ירמיה rejected: a smart ox makes the pit owner exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'בר דעת' means a smart ox, then the ברייתא really does exempt the owner for a smart ox. That would mean the משנה's list was meant to exclude smart oxen after all, which undercuts רבי ירמיה's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not...? (proposes a reading)

phrases.english: Rav Acha said to Ravina,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ בַּר דַּעַת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: but it was taught: if a mentally competent one fell into it, he is exempt.
What, does it not mean a mentally competent ox?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא לְרָבִינָא, וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses a ברייתא to challenge the conclusion of step 2 that a smart ox makes the owner liable.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה's claim that the pit owner is obviously liable for a smart ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says a 'בר דעת' that falls in makes the owner exempt, and that most naturally means a smart ox.

steps.title: רבינא: it means a person
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that the ברייתא's 'בר דעת' refers to a person, not an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא answered: No, it means a person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא deflects the challenge by saying the ברייתא is not talking about an ox at all but about a human being.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'בר דעת' means a person, the ברייתא says nothing about smart oxen, and רבי ירמיה's reading of the משנה stands.

phrases.english: He said to him: No, it means a person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא's challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining who the ברייתא is talking about

steps.title: Then would a person who is not competent make the owner liable?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא points out that reading it as a person implies a mentally incompetent person would make the owner liable, but the תורה only makes a pit owner liable for an ox, not a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then it is only a mentally competent person who makes the owner exempt, and a person who is not competent would make him liable? But the פסוק says 'ox', not a person!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא attacks רבינא's answer by showing the strange result it leads to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling it 'a competent person' suggests an incompetent person would make the owner liable. Yet the תורה makes a pit owner liable only for animals ('an ox'), never for a human of any kind. So the word 'בר דעת' would be pointless if it meant a person.

keyTerms.meaning: If that were so; then according to you
It is written in the פסוק

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, אָדָם בֶּן דַּעַת הוּא דְּפָטוּר,
phrases.english: If that is so, it is only a competent person for whom he is exempt,

phrases.aramaic: הָא לָאו בֶּן דַּעַת הוּא – דְּחַיָּיב?
phrases.english: but for one who is not competent, he would be liable?
"An ox" is written, and not a person!
phrases.notes: שמות 21:33: "וְנָפַל שָׁמָּה שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר".

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, אָדָם בֶּן דַּעַת הוּא דְּפָטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's answer in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's reading of 'בר דעת' as a person
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reading implies an incompetent person makes the owner liable, but the פסוק limits liability to an 'ox', excluding all humans.

steps.title: It means a species that is בן דעת
steps.stepSummary: The answer: 'בן דעת' describes the whole human species, which includes every person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what does 'בן דעת' mean? A species that is בן דעת, so all humans are included.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer fixes the problem from step 5 by explaining 'בן דעת' as a description of mankind as a whole, not of one individual.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Humans as a species have understanding, so the ברייתא means: if any human falls in, the owner is exempt. This covers even a human who is personally not competent, which removes the strange result from step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: A species that has understanding, meaning humans

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מַאי ״בֶּן דַּעַת״ – מִין בֶּן דַּעַת.
phrases.english: Rather, what does "competent" mean? A species that is competent.
phrases.notes: So 'בן דעת' describes human beings as a group. Any person, even one who is not competent, is included.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַאי בֶּן דַּעַת – מִין בֶּן דַּעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the term as describing a species
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'בן דעת' describes an individual person, implying an incompetent person would be different.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בן דעת' describes the human species, so every person is exempt.

steps.title: A ברייתא that says 'an ox that is בן דעת'
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא brings a ברייתא that explicitly says 'an ox that is בן דעת', so it cannot mean a human.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But a ברייתא teaches that if an ox that is בן דעת fell into it, the owner is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא blocks the 'human species' answer with a ברייתא that clearly names an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא says 'שור' outright, so it cannot be explained as a person or as mankind. It seems to say directly that a smart ox makes the pit owner exempt, which challenges רבי ירמיה again. The next step answers this: רבא accepts the ברייתא and drops רבי ירמיה's approach.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox that is mentally competent, a smart ox

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the matter ends here. This step is a challenge, and the גמרא's answer comes right after it.

phrases.english: He said to him: But it was taught:

phrases.aramaic: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר בֶּן דַּעַת – פָּטוּר!
phrases.english: if a competent ox fell into it, he is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, וְהָתַנְיָא: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר בֶּן דַּעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'species' answer of step 6 with a ברייתא that clearly mentions an ox.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'בן דעת' as humans, and רבי ירמיה's claim that a smart ox makes the owner liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly says 'an ox that is בן דעת' is exempt, so it cannot refer to people.

steps.title: רבא: Only a weak-minded ox makes the pit owner liable
steps.stepSummary: רבא sets aside the earlier answer and explains that the owner pays only for a deaf, foolish or very young ox. A normal alert ox should have looked where it was going, so the owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: an ox that is deaf, an ox that is foolish, an ox that is very young — only these make the owner liable. But a normal, alert ox — he is exempt. Why? Because it should have looked carefully as it walked.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא drops the earlier answer and gives a new way to deal with רב אחא's ברייתא about a smart ox. He says the owner pays only when an ox with weak awareness falls in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא from step 7 said a smart ox (בן דעת) does not make the owner liable. רבא agrees with that plainly: liability is limited to an ox that cannot protect itself. A normal ox is expected to look ahead, so if it falls, the fault is really its own.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule for the whole sugya: a בור owner is responsible only when the animal could not be expected to avoid the pit.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
An ox that is deaf,
an ox that is foolish,
an ox that is very young — specifically these;
but an ox that is alert — he is exempt.
What is the reason?
Because it should have looked carefully and walked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 7 by accepting that a smart ox exempts the owner, and replacing the earlier approach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: liability applies only to an ox lacking normal awareness.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every ox that falls into a בור makes the owner liable, so the ברייתא's 'smart ox' had to be explained away.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a deaf, foolish or very young ox makes the owner liable; a normal ox should have watched its step.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists a deaf, foolish, young, or blind ox, or one walking at night, as cases where the owner pays, and a normal ox walking by day as exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way: if a deaf, foolish, very young, or blind ox, or one walking at night, fell into it, he is liable. If it was alert and walking by day, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רבא said. This backs up his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא adds two more cases where the ox cannot see the danger: a blind ox and an ox walking at night. The common idea is that the owner pays only when the ox could not reasonably have avoided the pit.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא (a support)

steps.whatToRemember: The בור owner pays only if the ox could not see or understand the danger (deaf, foolish, young, blind, or at night). A normal ox walking by day — the owner is exempt.

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:

phrases.aramaic: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר חֵרֵשׁ, שׁוֹטֶה, וְקָטָן,
phrases.english: If there fell into it an ox that is deaf, foolish, or very young,
phrases.notes: "Into it" means into the pit.

phrases.english: or blind, or walking at night — he is liable.
Alert and walking by day — he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's answer from step 8.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's rule that only a weak-minded ox makes the owner liable.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing liable and exempt cases.

steps.title: New משנה: Many 'ox' laws apply to every animal
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists eight laws where an ox and any other animal are the same: falling into a pit, keeping away from הר סיני, paying double, returning lost items, unloading, muzzling, mixing kinds, and שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox and any animal are the same for: falling into a pit, keeping away from הר סיני, paying double, returning a lost item, unloading, muzzling, mixing kinds, and שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It says that in eight areas of law, any animal is treated just like an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of these laws is written in the תורה using the words 'ox' or 'donkey'. The משנה teaches that those words are not a limit; every animal is included.

keyTerms.meaning: Muzzling an animal while it works

phrases.english: MISHNA:
Both an ox and any animal are the same —
for falling into a pit,
and for keeping away from Mount Sinai,
and for double payment,
and for returning a lost item,
for unloading, for muzzling,
for mixing kinds, and for Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, moving on from the discussion of which ox makes a בור owner liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In eight areas of law, any animal has the same law as an ox.

steps.title: Wild animals and birds too; the תורה spoke of the usual case
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds that wild animals and birds are the same. It asks why the תורה says 'ox or donkey' and answers that the תורה just spoke about the common case.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so too wild animals and birds are like them. If so, why does it say 'ox or donkey'? Only because the verse spoke about what is common.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה widens the rule to wild animals and birds. Then it asks and answers its own question about why the פסוקים mention only an ox or donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every creature is included, the words 'ox or donkey' seem unneeded. The answer is that the תורה used the most common example people deal with, not to exclude other animals.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse spoke about the usual case

steps.confusionAlert: 'Ox or donkey' in these פסוקים is an example, not a limit. Don't read it as excluding other animals.

phrases.english: And so too wild animals and birds are like them.

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן, לָמָּה נֶאֱמַר ״שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר״?
phrases.english: If so, why does it say "ox or donkey"?
Only because the verse spoke about what is common.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה, extending the rule and explaining the wording of the פסוקים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wild animals and birds share these laws; 'ox or donkey' is just the common example.

steps.title: Source for any animal in a pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that the פסוק 'he shall pay money to its owners' includes any animal that has an owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: For falling into a pit — it is written 'he shall pay money to its owners': anything that has owners, as we said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins giving a source for each law in the משנה. First: any owned animal that falls into a pit is included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק focuses on paying the owner, not on what kind of animal it was. So any animal with an owner counts, as the גמרא explained earlier.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall pay money to its owners

phrases.english: GEMARA:
For falling into a pit —
"He shall pay money to its owners" is written —
phrases.notes: שמות 21:34

phrases.english: anything that has owners,
as we said.
phrases.notes: This points back to the earlier discussion on 54a.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִנְפִילַת הַבּוֹר כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining the sources for the list in the משנה of step 10.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's rule that any animal falling into a בור makes the owner liable.

steps.title: Source for all creatures keeping away from הר סיני
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'whether animal or man, it shall not live' covers domestic animals, wild animals are included in 'animal', and the word 'whether' adds birds.
steps.simpleTranslation: For keeping away from הר סיני — 'whether animal or man, it shall not live'; a wild animal is included in 'animal'; and 'whether' comes to include birds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source that every creature had to stay away from הר סיני.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בהמה in the פסוק already covers wild animals too. The extra word אם is read as adding birds, which would not otherwise be included.

phrases.english: For keeping away from Mount Sinai —
"Whether animal or man, it shall not live,"
phrases.notes: שמות 19:13

phrases.english: and a wild animal is included in "animal";
"whether" — to include the birds.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְהַפְרָשַׁת הַר סִינַי אִם בְּהֵמָה אִם אִישׁ לֹא יִחְיֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues down the משנה's list, giving the source for the second law.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's rule that all animals and birds had to keep away from הר סיני.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'אם בהמה אם איש לא יחיה', with the extra word אם.

steps.title: Double payment applies to any animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that תשלומי כפל covers every animal, because the פסוק says 'for any matter of trespass.'
steps.simpleTranslation: For double payment: as we say, 'for any matter of trespass' is a general phrase that includes every kind of wrongdoing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next item on the משנה's list, the double payment a thief owes, and shows it applies to any animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about a thief paying double lists an ox, a donkey, a sheep, and a garment. But it also says 'על כל דבר פשע', 'for any matter of trespass.' The word 'כל' makes the rule general, so it covers stealing any animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Double payment, the penalty a thief pays
It made a general statement, it includes everything
As we say, pointing to a known teaching

phrases.english: For double payment: as we say,
'For any matter of trespass':
phrases.notes: שמות 22:8

phrases.english: it included every matter of wrongdoing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finding sources for the pit and הר סיני, the גמרא continues to the next item on the משנה's list.
steps.raayaObject: That תשלומי כפל applies to all animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: The general phrase 'על כל דבר פשע' (שמות 22:8)

steps.title: Returning a lost item applies to any animal
steps.stepSummary: השבת אבידה covers every animal because the פסוק says 'every lost thing of your brother.'
steps.simpleTranslation: For returning a lost item: the פסוק says 'for every lost thing of your brother.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source that the מצוה of returning lost things applies to any animal, not just an ox or sheep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק mentions a donkey and a garment, but then says 'לכל אבדת אחיך', 'every lost thing of your brother.' That broad wording covers every animal and every object.

keyTerms.meaning: For every, a word that widens the rule
Your brother, meaning a fellow Jew

phrases.english: For returning a lost item:
'For every lost thing of your brother.'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:3

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item on the משנה's list, again proven from broad wording in the פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That השבת אבידה applies to all animals

steps.title: Unloading is learned from שבת through the word 'donkey'
steps.stepSummary: פריקה applies to any animal, learned through a word-link (גזירה שוה) of 'donkey' and 'donkey' from the laws of שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: For unloading: we learn 'donkey' from 'donkey' in the laws of שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The פסוק about unloading only says 'donkey,' so the גמרא uses a word-link to the laws of שבת to show it covers every animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new kind of proof. There is no broad word in the unloading פסוק itself. Instead, the word 'חמור' also appears in the שבת command about resting animals. That command covers all animals, so unloading does too.

keyTerms.meaning: Unloading a burden from a fallen animal
Learning one law from another because they share the same word

steps.confusionAlert: Here the proof does not come from the unloading פסוק itself. It comes from matching the same word in a completely different topic, שבת.

phrases.english: For unloading:
he learns 'donkey'-'donkey' from שבת.
phrases.notes: 'Donkey' appears in the unloading פסוק (שמות 23:5) and in the שבת rest command (דברים 5:14), which covers all animals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from proofs based on broad wording to a word-link with שבת.
steps.raayaObject: That פריקה applies to all animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: A גזירה שוה of 'חמור' with the laws of שבת

steps.title: Muzzling is learned from שבת through the word 'ox'
steps.stepSummary: The ban on muzzling applies to any animal, learned through the word 'ox' that also appears in the laws of שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: For muzzling: we learn 'ox' from 'ox' in the laws of שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The muzzling פסוק only says 'ox,' so the גמרא again links it to the שבת command to include every animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Same method as the step before, but the shared word is now 'שור'. The שבת command mentions an ox and covers all animals, so the muzzling ban covers all animals too.

keyTerms.meaning: Muzzling an animal while it works with food

phrases.english: For muzzling:
phrases.notes: The פסוק is 'You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing' (דברים 25:4).

phrases.english: he learns 'ox'-'ox' from שבת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same שבת word-link method as פריקה, now with the word 'ox'.
steps.raayaObject: That the ban on חסימה applies to all animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: A גזירה שוה of 'שור' with the laws of שבת

steps.title: Both kinds of mixing are learned from שבת
steps.stepSummary: כלאים has two forms, plowing with two kinds and crossbreeding, and each is linked to שבת by a different shared word.
steps.simpleTranslation: For mixed kinds: if it means plowing with mixed kinds, we learn 'ox' from 'ox' in שבת. If it means crossbreeding, we learn 'your animal' from 'your animal' in שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא splits כלאים into two laws and gives a שבת word-link for each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plowing with an ox and a donkey together uses the word 'שור', which matches the שבת command. Crossbreeding uses the word 'בהמתך', which also appears in the שבת command. Either way, the law reaches every animal.
steps.whatToRemember: For each law in the משנה's list, the גמרא finds a source that it covers all animals: either broad wording like 'כל' in the פסוק, or a word-link to שבת, whose rest command covers every animal.

phrases.english: For mixed kinds:
if it is mixed kinds of plowing,
phrases.notes: Plowing with an ox and a donkey together (דברים 22:10).

phrases.english: he learns 'ox'-'ox' from שבת;
if it is mixed kinds of crossbreeding,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:19

phrases.english: he learns 'your animal'-'your animal' from שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְכִלְאַיִם אִי כִּלְאַיִם דַּחֲרִישָׁה יָלֵיף שׁוֹר שׁוֹר מִשַּׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the שבת word-link method, now dividing כלאים into two separate cases.
steps.raayaObject: That both kinds of כלאים apply to all animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: A גזירה שוה with שבת: 'שור' for plowing and 'בהמתך' for crossbreeding

steps.title: How do we know this about שבת itself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that 'ox and donkey' in the laws of שבת include all creatures.
steps.simpleTranslation: And regarding שבת, from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move. Every word-link so far pointed back to שבת, so now it asks what the source is for שבת itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proofs in steps 16-18 only work if 'ox' and 'donkey' in the שבת verses already mean every kind of creature. If that is not proven, those word-links teach nothing. So the גמרא has to find the base source.

keyTerms.meaning: from where do we know it?

phrases.english: And regarding שבת, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: He means: how do we know that 'ox' and 'donkey' in the שבת verses include every kind of creature?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the base source that the earlier word-links depend on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that 'ox and donkey' in the שבת verses cover all creatures.

steps.title: The two versions of the עשרת הדברות
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי, quoting רבי ישמעאל, says the second version names ox and donkey even though 'all your animals' already includes them. This teaches that ox and donkey stand for wild animals and birds too.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי יוסי says in the name of רבי ישמעאל: In the first עשרת הדברות it says 'your servant, your maidservant and your animal.' In the second it says 'your ox, your donkey and all your animals.' Aren't ox and donkey already part of 'all animals'? So why were they named separately? To teach you: just as with the ox and donkey mentioned here, wild animals and birds are treated like them, so too wherever ox and donkey are mentioned, all wild animals and birds are treated like them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. It points out that the second version lists 'ox and donkey' when they were not needed, and it learns a rule from that extra wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ox and donkey already fall under 'all your animals.' Naming them anyway shows that they are examples standing for every creature, and that holds wherever the תורה mentions them. That is what made the word-links in steps 16-18 work.

keyTerms.meaning: the first version of the עשרת הדברות, in שמות
the second version of the עשרת הדברות, in דברים
just like them, with the same law

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the base source that the earlier word-links (steps 16-18) rely on.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says in the name of Rabbi Yishmael:
In the first Commandments it is stated:
'Your manservant, your maidservant, and your animal,'
phrases.notes: שמות 20:10

phrases.english: and in the latter Commandments it is stated:
'And your ox, and your donkey, and all your animals.'
phrases.notes: דברים 5:14

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲלֹא שׁוֹר וַחֲמוֹר בִּכְלַל כׇּל בְּהֵמָה הָיוּ,
phrases.english: Weren't ox and donkey already included in 'all animals'?
So why were they singled out?
To tell you:
Just as with the ox and donkey stated here,
wild animals and birds are just like them,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל חַיָּה וָעוֹף כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן.
phrases.english: so too all wild animals and birds are just like them.
phrases.notes: Meaning: in every other place where the תורה says 'ox' or 'donkey.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra 'ox and donkey' in the second version, written next to 'all your animals,' shows they stand for all creatures, including wild animals and birds.

steps.title: Maybe it is a general term followed by a detail
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests reading 'animal' in the first version as a general term (כלל) and 'ox and donkey' as a detail (פרט). Then only ox and donkey would be included.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say this instead: 'animal' in the first version is a general term, and 'your ox and your donkey' in the second version is a detail. With a general term followed by a detail, the general term includes only what is in the detail. So ox and donkey yes, anything else no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא with a standard rule for reading פסוקים. That rule would give the opposite result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the rule of כלל ופרט, a detail that comes after a general term limits it. So 'animal' would shrink down to only ox and donkey, instead of ox and donkey growing to include everything.

keyTerms.meaning: a general term in a פסוק
a specific detail in a פסוק
a general term followed by a detail: only the detail is included

steps.confusionAlert: Here the כלל comes from the first version (שמות) and the פרט comes from the second version (דברים). The גמרא is reading the two versions together as one sequence.

phrases.english: Say instead:
'Animal' of the first Commandments is a general term,
'your ox and your donkey' of the latter Commandments is a detail;
a general term followed by a detail:
the general term contains only what is in the detail;
ox and donkey, yes,
anything else, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that ox and donkey include all creatures.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under כלל ופרט the detail limits the general term, so only ox and donkey would be included.

steps.title: A second general term widens it to all living creatures
steps.stepSummary: 'And all your animals' comes after the detail, so this is a כלל ופרט וכלל. That pattern includes everything similar to the detail, meaning all living creatures.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: 'and all your animals' in the second version goes back and generalizes again. With a general term, a detail and a general term, you include only things similar to the detail. Just as the detail is clearly living creatures, so too all living creatures are included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is another general term after the detail. That changes which rule applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלל ופרט וכלל does not limit things to the detail alone. It includes whatever is similar to the detail. Since ox and donkey are living creatures, every living creature is included.

keyTerms.meaning: it went back and generalized again
general, detail, general: include things similar to the detail

phrases.english: They said:
'And all your animals' of the latter Commandments:
it went back and generalized.
A general term, a detail and a general term:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט;
phrases.english: you may only include what is like the detail;
just as the detail is clearly living creatures,
so too all living creatures.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points out a second general term, which changes the rule being used.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It is a כלל ופרט, so only ox and donkey are included.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is a כלל ופרט וכלל, so all living creatures, which are similar to the detail, are included.

steps.title: Maybe the shared trait is a carcass that makes things טמא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: maybe the trait the detail teaches is 'a creature whose carcass makes a person טמא by touching or carrying.' That would leave out birds.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead: just as the detail is clearly something whose carcass makes a person טמא by touching and carrying, so too everything whose carcass makes a person טמא by touching and carrying is included. But birds, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל but questions which trait of the detail we should copy. A narrower trait would leave out birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With כלל ופרט וכלל, you include whatever is similar to the detail, but 'similar' depends on which trait you pick. Ox and donkey also share that their carcass makes a person טמא by touch and by carrying, which birds do not. Using that trait would cut birds out, against the ברייתא's claim.

keyTerms.meaning: the carcass of an animal that died without proper שחיטה
makes a person טמא by touching

phrases.english: But say instead:
just as the detail is clearly
something whose carcass makes one impure by touching and by carrying,
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is added in the corrected wording. It doesn't change the meaning.

phrases.aramaic: אַף כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁנְּבָלָתוֹ מְטַמְּאָ[ה] בְּמַגָּע וּבְמַשָּׂא;
phrases.english: so too everything whose carcass makes one impure by touching and by carrying;
but birds, no!
phrases.notes: A bird's carcass doesn't make a person impure by touching or carrying, so birds would not fit this trait.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges which trait of the detail the answer in step 22 should use.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 22, which includes all living creatures, including birds.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The detail could be defined more narrowly, as creatures whose carcass makes a person טמא by touching and carrying, and that would leave out birds.

steps.title: Two details show the trait is wider
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer step 23: if the תורה only meant animals whose carcass is טמא, one detail would have been enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: If so, the תורה should have written just one detail!
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים answer the challenge from step 23. They argue that the תורה wrote two details, so the trait must be wider than 'carcass that makes טמא'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ox and donkey both have carcasses that make a person טמא. If that were the only point, naming one of them would teach it. Since the תורה names both, the second detail must widen the trait, so birds can be included.

phrases.english: They said: If so,
phrases.notes: 'If so' means: if the trait were only animals whose carcass makes a person טמא, as step 23 suggested.

phrases.english: let the Merciful One write one detail!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא חַד פְּרָטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording: the second detail would be unneeded under the narrow reading.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The trait might be only animals whose carcass makes a person טמא, which leaves out birds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two details mean the trait is broader, so birds are included.

steps.title: Each detail is needed for its own reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: ox alone and donkey alone would each teach something too narrow, so both are needed even under the narrow reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which one should the תורה write? If it wrote only 'ox,' I would say only animals offered on the מזבח are included and others are not, so it wrote 'donkey.' If it wrote only 'donkey,' I would say only animals whose firstborn is holy are included and others are not, so it wrote 'ox.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the answer of step 24. It shows that the תורה needed to write both details, so the second one is not extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With only 'ox', we would limit the law to animals that are offered on the מזבח. With only 'donkey', we would limit it to animals whose firstborn is holy. Each detail is needed to stop the other from being read too narrowly, so neither is extra, and step 23's challenge about birds comes back.

phrases.english: Which one should the Merciful One write?
If the Merciful One wrote only "ox," I would have said:
an animal that is offered on the altar, yes,
one that is not offered on the altar, no;
so the Merciful One wrote "donkey."
And if the Merciful One wrote only "donkey," I would have said:
an animal whose firstborn is holy, yes,
phrases.notes: A firstborn donkey has to be redeemed with a lamb (שמות 13:13). That is the holiness meant here.

phrases.english: one whose firstborn is not holy, no;
so the Merciful One wrote "ox."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the second detail is extra.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Each detail on its own would narrow the law to its own special trait, so both are needed anyway.

steps.title: 'And all your animals' is an including word
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא takes a new approach: 'וכל בהמתך' is a ריבוי, a word that includes broadly, not a כלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, 'and all your animals' is an amplification.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the two-details argument failed, the גמרא answers a different way. It reads the word 'וכל' as a ריבוי instead of a כלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כלל ופרט וכלל includes only things similar to the details. A ריבוי includes much more widely, so it does not depend on finding a trait that birds share. This brings birds back in.

keyTerms.meaning: An amplification, a word that includes broadly

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up a כלל and a ריבוי. Both can come from the word כל, but a ריבוי includes much more broadly than a כלל ופרט וכלל.

phrases.english: Rather, "and all your animals" is an amplification.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new answer to step 23 after step 25 rejected the first one.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes the method of reading the verse, from כלל ופרט to ריבוי.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'וכל' is a כלל, so only things like the details are included, and birds might be left out.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'וכל' is a ריבוי that includes broadly, so birds are included.

steps.title: Is every 'כל' really a ריבוי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: with מעשר, the word כל is read as a כלל in a כלל ופרט, not as a ריבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is every place the תורה writes 'all' an amplification? But with מעשר, where 'all' is written, we explain it as a general term and a detail!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new answer from step 26. It points to מעשר, where the same word כל is read as a כלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If כל always meant ריבוי, it would have to mean that by מעשר too. But there we use כלל ופרט. So why read it as a ריבוי here?

keyTerms.meaning: A general term and a detail

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל הֵיכָא דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״כֹּל״ – רִיבּוּיָא הוּא?!
phrases.english: And is every place the Merciful One writes "all" an amplification?!
But regarding tithes, where "all" is written,
phrases.notes: This is the money of מעשר שני, which the next step shows is spent on food in ירושלים.

phrases.english: we explain it as a general term and a detail!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֹל הֵיכָא דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״כֹּל״ – רִיבּוּיָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'וכל' is a ריבוי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By מעשר the same word כל is read as a כלל, so כל is not automatically a ריבוי.

steps.title: The ברייתא on spending מעשר money
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that reads the מעשר שני verse as כלל, פרט, and כלל again.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'And you shall spend the money on all that your soul desires' is a general term. 'On cattle, sheep, wine, and strong drink' is a detail. 'And on all that your soul asks of you' goes back and makes a general term again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge by quoting a ברייתא. The ברייתא shows that 'בכל' in the מעשר verse is treated as a כלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse has the same shape as ours: 'all', then specific items, then 'all' again. The ברייתא calls it a כלל ופרט וכלל, not a ריבוי. This supports the question of step 27.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
It went back and made a general statement again

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: ״וְנָתַתָּה הַכֶּסֶף בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תְּאַוֶּה נַפְשְׁךָ״ – כָּלַל,
phrases.english: As it was taught: "And you shall give the money for all that your soul desires" is a general term,
phrases.notes: דברים 14:26

phrases.english: "for cattle, for sheep, for wine, and for strong drink" is a detail,
"and for all that your soul asks of you" goes back and makes a general term again;

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: ״וְנָתַתָּה הַכֶּסֶף בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תְּאַוֶּה נַפְשְׁךָ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source behind the challenge of step 27.
steps.raayaObject: That כל by מעשר is read as a כלל in a כלל ופרט וכלל.

steps.title: The ברייתא finishes: only things like the detail are included
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא applies the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל to the מעשר שני verse. Only things similar to the listed items may be bought: things that come from something that grew, and that get their food from the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: A general statement, a detail, and another general statement: you only include things similar to the detail. Just as the detail lists things that are produce of produce and grown from the ground, so too, anything that is produce of produce and grown from the ground may be bought.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 28 finishes its reasoning and states what the כלל ופרט וכלל teaches about מעשר שני money. This completes the proof against reading כל as a ריבוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under כלל ופרט וכלל, the general words do not include everything. They only widen the list to things that share the features of the detail. Since the word כל here works as part of that pattern, the challenge from step 27 now stands: כל seems to be a כלל, not a ריבוי.

keyTerms.meaning: A general term, a specific list, then a general term again. You include only things similar to the list.

keyTerms.term: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט
keyTerms.meaning: You may only include things that are like the detail
Produce of produce: something born from or growing out of something else that grew
Things that grow from the ground or get their food from it

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the proof behind the קשיא of step 27. Here כל is clearly treated as a כלל, so the גמרא must explain why כל in the שבת verse can be read differently.

phrases.english: A general statement, a detail, and a general statement:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט,
phrases.english: you may only include what is similar to the detail.
Just as the detail is clearly defined
as produce of produce and things grown from the ground,
phrases.notes: The detail is cattle, sheep, wine and beer. Animals are born from animals, and wine comes from grapes, and all of them get their food from the ground.

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל פְּרִי מִפְּרִי וְגִידּוּלֵי קַרְקַע!
phrases.english: so too, anything that is produce of produce and grown from the ground!

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted in step 28
steps.raayaObject: That the word כל is read as a כלל, not a ריבוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about the מעשר שני verse (דברים 14:26)

steps.title: 'בכל' is a general statement, but 'כל' is an inclusion
steps.stepSummary: The answer separates two words. In the מעשר שני verse the word is בכל, which works as a כלל. In the שבת verse the word is כל, which works as a ריבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: 'For anything' (בכל) is a general statement. 'Any' (כל) is an inclusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from the מעשר שני ברייתא by pointing out that the word there is slightly different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof only works if the two words act the same way. This answer says they do not: בכל, with the extra letter ב, is read as a כלל, while plain כל is read as a ריבוי. So the ברייתא does not stop us from reading וכל בהמתך broadly.

keyTerms.meaning: They say. Introduces an answer from the scholars.
A general statement, used in a כלל ופרט pattern
An inclusion: a word that widens the law very broadly

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up a כלל and a ריבוי. A כלל ופרט includes only things like the detail, but a ריבוי includes almost everything. That is why it matters which one כל is.

phrases.english: They say: 'For anything' is a general statement;
'Any' is an inclusion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof from the ברייתא in steps 28–29
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought בכל in the מעשר שני verse and כל in the שבת verse work the same way
steps.terutzMaskana: בכל is a כלל, but כל is a ריבוי, so וכל בהמתך includes broadly

steps.title: Even if 'כל' is usually a general statement, here the extra word makes it an inclusion
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: maybe כל is normally a כלל too. But in the שבת verse the תורה could have just said 'your animal', as it did in the first version of the עשרת הדברות. Adding 'any' shows it is a ריבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you prefer, say: 'any' is also a general statement. But this 'any' here is an inclusion, because the תורה could have written 'and your animal', as in the first version of the עשרת הדברות. Instead it wrote 'and any of your animals'. Learn from this that it is an inclusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to answer: it accepts that כל can be a כלל, but proves that in this verse it is a ריבוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not separate בכל from כל. Instead it compares the two versions of the עשרת הדברות. The first says only ובהמתך. The second adds וכל, and that extra word shows the תורה meant to include broadly.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say. Introduces a second, different answer.
The first version of the עשרת הדברות, in שמות
Since it could have written. Points out that the Torah chose extra words on purpose.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
'Any' is also a general statement,
but this 'any' here is an inclusion;
since it could have written: 'And your animal,'
as is written in the first Commandments,
phrases.notes: שמות 20:10

phrases.english: and instead it wrote: 'And any of your animals,'
phrases.notes: דברים 5:14

phrases.english: learn from this that it is an inclusion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the same challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proving a ריבוי from extra wording, by comparing the two versions of the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If כל is normally a כלל, then וכל בהמתך should be read narrowly
steps.terutzMaskana: The added word וכל, missing in the first version, shows that here it is a ריבוי
steps.whatToRemember: Both answers reach the same result: וכל בהמתך in the שבת verse is a ריבוי that includes all animals.

steps.title: If 'כל' includes everything, why name specific animals?
steps.stepSummary: If וכל בהמתך already includes every animal, why does the Torah also say 'your animal' in the first version and 'ox and donkey' in the second version?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you say 'any' is an inclusion, why do I need 'your animal' in the first Commandments, and 'ox and donkey' in the last Commandments?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the גמרא has decided כל is a ריבוי, it asks why the other animal words in the verses are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ריבוי already covers every animal. So the separate words seem extra, and the תורה does not waste words. The גמרא now has to find a purpose for each one.

keyTerms.meaning: Now that you have said. Builds a new question on the answer just given.
The second version of the עשרת הדברות, in דברים
Why do I need it? Asks why a word seems extra.

phrases.english: Now that you have said that 'any' is an inclusion,
'your animal' of the first Commandments,
and 'ox and donkey' of the last Commandments,
why do I need them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the conclusion that כל is a ריבוי
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of וכל בהמתך as a ריבוי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If כל includes all animals, the specific words בהמתך, שור and חמור appear to teach nothing

steps.title: 'Ox' is needed to link שבת with the law of muzzling
steps.stepSummary: The answer starts: the word שור is needed for a גזירה שוה. The word 'ox' appears both in the שבת verse and in the law against muzzling an animal while it works.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: 'Ox' is needed to teach a link, 'ox' and 'ox', for muzzling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts explaining why each extra word is needed, beginning with שור. The next step finishes the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה connects two laws that use the same word. Because שור appears both in the שבת verse and in the muzzling verse, the law of muzzling can learn from שבת. So the word שור is not extra, even though כל already includes all animals.

keyTerms.meaning: A link between two laws that use the same word in the Torah
Muzzling: blocking an animal's mouth while it works so it cannot eat

phrases.english: They say: 'Ox' is needed
to teach 'ox'–'ox' for muzzling,
phrases.notes: The muzzling verse is דברים 25:4. The same word 'ox' in both places links the two laws.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 32
steps.terutzResolutionType: Giving the seemingly extra word a purpose through a גזירה שוה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word שור seemed extra, because כל already covers all animals
steps.terutzMaskana: שור is needed to connect שבת with the law of muzzling

steps.title: Donkey teaches unloading, your animal teaches mixed species
steps.stepSummary: The answer continues. The word חמור in the שבת verse is needed for a גזירה שוה about פריקה. The word בהמתך is needed for a גזירה שוה about כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'donkey' is there to teach a link between 'donkey' and 'donkey' for the law of unloading. The word 'your animal' is there to teach a link between 'your animal' and 'your animal' for the law of mixed species.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer to the question in step 32. Just as שור was needed for a link to muzzling, חמור and בהמתך are each needed to link to other laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was: if וכל בהמתך already covers every animal, why list specific animals? The answer is that each listed word is not extra. Each one builds a bridge to a different law. חמור connects to the מצוה of פריקה, and בהמתך connects to the איסור of כלאים, so whatever is true of animals for שבת carries over to those laws.

keyTerms.meaning: the מצוה to help unload a fallen animal's burden
the איסור of working or breeding two different species together

steps.confusionAlert: These words are not extra and they do not shrink the rule. וכל בהמתך still includes every animal. The specific words are there only to build links to other laws.

phrases.english: "Donkey" is there to teach a link between "donkey" and "donkey" for unloading,
phrases.notes: The two verses are שמות 23:5, about unloading, and דברים 5:14, the שבת verse.

phrases.english: "Your animal" is there to teach a link between "your animal" and "your animal" for mixed species.
phrases.notes: The two verses are ויקרא 19:19, about mixed species, and שמות 20:10, the שבת verse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun in step 33 by explaining the remaining words, חמור and בהמתך.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each seemingly extra word is needed for its own גזירה שוה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The specific animal words look extra once וכל בהמתך includes every animal.
steps.terutzMaskana: שור links to muzzling, חמור links to פריקה, and בהמתך links to כלאים. None of the words is wasted.

steps.title: Then a person should be forbidden to plow with an animal
steps.stepSummary: If כלאים is learned from the שבת verse, and that verse also lists people, then a person should also be forbidden to work together with an animal. Yet a משנה says a person may plow and pull with any animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even a person should be forbidden! Why then did we learn in a משנה: A person is permitted to plow and pull together with any of them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the link between שבת and כלאים. The link seems to prove too much.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שבת verse puts people, such as you, your servant and your maidservant, side by side with animals. If כלאים is connected to that verse, people and animals should count as 'different species' that may not work together. But a משנה clearly allows a person to plow alongside an animal.

keyTerms.meaning: why then did we learn (in a משנה)?
to plow and to pull (a load)

phrases.english: If so, even a person should be forbidden!
phrases.notes: He means a person working together with an animal, because the שבת verse lists people right next to the animals.

phrases.english: Why then did we learn:
A person is permitted with all of them
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in כלאים 8:6. 'All of them' means all the animals.

phrases.english: to plow and to pull?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ אָדָם לִיתְּסַר! אַלְּמָה תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the בהמתך link to כלאים proposed in step 34 by showing it leads to a result that contradicts a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The link between the שבת verse and כלאים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The שבת verse groups people together with animals. If כלאים draws from it, people and animals should be forbidden to work together, but the משנה in כלאים permits this.

steps.title: People are compared to animals only for resting
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the scholars of פפוניא, meaning רב אחא בר יעקב, know the reason. The verse says 'so that your servant and maidservant may rest like you,' which shows that people were compared to animals only for resting on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The scholars of פפוניא know the reason for this. Who is that? רב אחא בר יעקב. The verse says: 'So that your servant and your maidservant may rest like you.' This means: I compared them only for resting, and not for anything else.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question about people and animals. The Torah itself limits the comparison to resting on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The end of the שבת verse explains its purpose: everyone listed should rest. So putting people next to animals in that verse is only about the law of resting. It does not make people and animals one group for other laws, so כלאים does not apply to a person working with an animal.

keyTerms.meaning: the scholars of the town of Paphunya
I compared them (an equation drawn from the verse)

steps.whatToRemember: Each animal word in the שבת verse links to its own law: שור to muzzling, חמור to פריקה, and בהמתך to כלאים. People appear in the same verse, but they are compared to animals only for resting on שבת. That is why a person may plow together with an animal.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the purpose a verse states for itself can limit how far a comparison drawn from it can reach.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
The scholars of Paphunya know the reason for this matter.
And who is that? Rav Acha bar Yaakov.
The verse says:
"So that your servant and your maidservant may rest like you."
phrases.notes: דברים 5:14

phrases.english: For resting I compared them,
phrases.notes: The תורה is speaking here: people are put next to animals only for the purpose of resting.

phrases.english: and not for anything else.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: פַּפּוּנָאֵי יָדְעִי טַעְמָא דְּהָא מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 35 by limiting the comparison between people and animals.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the comparison based on the verse's own stated purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because people and animals are listed together in the שבת verse, they would be treated as one group for כלאים too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse compares people to animals only for resting on שבת. So כלאים does not forbid a person from working with an animal.

steps.title: Why is 'good' missing from the first version of the עשרת הדברות?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בן עגיל asks רבי חייא בר אבא why the word 'good' does not appear in the first version of the עשרת הדברות, while it does appear in the later version.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בן עגיל asked רבי חייא בר אבא: Why is the word 'good' not said in the first version of the עשרת הדברות, while in the later version of the עשרת הדברות...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question that compares the two versions of the עשרת הדברות. The question is only beginning here and finishes in the next lines, so this step sets up what comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps looked at a difference between the versions in the שבת command, such as 'your animal' versus 'ox and donkey'. Now רבי חנינא בן עגיל points to a different difference: the word 'good' appears only in the later version. He wants to know why the first version leaves it out.

keyTerms.meaning: The first version of the Ten Commandments (in שמות)
The later version of the Ten Commandments (in דברים)

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Agil asked
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba:
For what reason, in the first version of the Commandments,
phrases.notes: The first version is the one in שמות. The later version is the one in דברים.

phrases.english: is the word 'good' not stated in them,
whereas in the later version of the Commandments,

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן עָגֵיל אֶת רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the differences in the שבת command, discussed in steps 32 to 36, to a new difference between the two versions of the עשרת הדברות: the word 'good'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the first version of the עשרת הדברות leave out the word 'good', while the later version includes it?
